title: Gateway API
summary: Role-oriented successor to Ingress: GatewayClass, Gateway and HTTPRoute, how they link, and how a request flows.

blocks.text: Some ports outgrow the old main gate and install the **newer gate system** (Gateway API). It is not built into the harbor office: you add its new kinds of forms to the ledger (CRDs) or follow your installer's steps. Many contractors build it, so the same forms work at many ports, though each has its own quirks worth reading about.
Gateway API is a family of API kinds for **dynamic infrastructure provisioning** and **advanced traffic routing**. It is an **add-on**: Kubernetes doesn't implement it natively.

items: Its kinds are defined as **Custom Resources**. You install the Gateway API CRDs, or follow your chosen implementation's install steps.
Many implementations support it, so the same specs work in many places.
Read your implementation's docs for its caveats.
API group and version in the examples: `gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1`.

blocks.text: The new gate system is organised around who does what. The **city** (infrastructure provider) supplies gate types for many ports, the **port authority** (cluster operator) sets policy and access, and **tenants** (application developers) configure their own apps. Each role gets its own forms. Fancy routing, like matching on headers or splitting traffic by weight, is built in rather than scribbled on sticky notes as with the old gate.

rows: Infrastructure that lets many isolated clusters serve many tenants (e.g. a cloud provider)
Policies, network access and application permissions for clusters

items: **Role-oriented:** the API kinds mirror these organisational roles.
**Portable:** specs are custom resources supported by many implementations.
**Expressive:** header-based matching, traffic weighting and more are built in. With Ingress these needed custom annotations.
**Extensible:** custom resources can be linked at various layers of the API.

blocks.text: Picture the pieces: a **gate design** (GatewayClass) run by a contractor, an actual **gate** built from it (Gateway), and **tenant route cards** (HTTPRoute, GRPCRoute) that map visitors to port phone numbers (Services). Each gate follows exactly one design. Route cards attach to a gate, and the gate can choose which cards it accepts, so both sides must agree before visitors flow.

rows: A set of Gateways with common config, managed by the controller that implements the class
An instance of traffic handling infrastructure, e.g. a cloud load balancer or in-cluster proxy
HTTP rules mapping traffic from a Gateway listener to backends (often Services)
The same idea for gRPC traffic

steps.text: A **GatewayClass** defines a type of gateway, run by a controller. The infrastructure provider manages it.
A **Gateway** is an instance of traffic-handling infrastructure, such as a load balancer. The cluster operator manages it.
An **HTTPRoute** attaches to a Gateway and maps requests to backends. Application developers manage it.
A request reaches the Gateway, matches a route rule and is sent to the backend Service.

items: These four kinds are **stable**.
Each Gateway is linked to **exactly one** GatewayClass, which names the controller that manages it.
One or more Routes (such as HTTPRoute) attach to a Gateway.
A Gateway can filter which Routes may attach to its listeners. Together this forms a **bidirectional trust model** between Gateways and Routes.

blocks.text: The city files a gate design whose `controllerName` tells a contractor "this one's yours". The port authority then builds a gate citing that design (`gatewayClassName`) and opens doors (listeners), each with a name, protocol and port. If you don't assign an address, the contractor gives the gate one. By default a gate only accepts route cards from its own company yard (namespace); `allowedRoutes` opens it to others.

apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: GatewayClass
metadata:
  name: <class-name>
spec:
  controllerName: <controller-name>
---
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: <gateway-name>
  namespace: <namespace>
spec:
  gatewayClassName: <class-name>
  listeners:
  - name: http
    protocol: HTTP
    port: 80
    hostname: "<host>"
    allowedRoutes:
      namespaces:
        from: Same

items: A GatewayClass's `controllerName` tells an implementation which classes it manages.
A Gateway must reference a GatewayClass through `gatewayClassName`.
Each **listener** has a name, protocol and port; the example listener also sets a hostname and `allowedRoutes`.
If `addresses` is left unset, the implementation's controller assigns an address or hostname to the Gateway.

blocks.text: By default a Gateway only accepts Routes **from its own namespace**. To attach Routes from other namespaces, configure `allowedRoutes` on the listener.

A tenant fills in a route card (HTTPRoute) that names its gate (`parentRefs`), the host names and paths it handles (`hostnames`, `matches`), and where visitors go (`backendRefs`). Filing the card reconfigures the gate itself. A gRPC route card works the same way. The card only counts if the gate is real, the gate's design exists, and the door's `allowedRoutes` admits the tenant's yard.

apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: <route-name>
spec:
  parentRefs:
  - name: <gateway-name>
  hostnames:
  - "<host>"
  rules:
  - matches:
    - path:
        type: PathPrefix
        value: /<path>
    backendRefs:
    - name: <service-name>
      port: <port>

items: `parentRefs` attaches the Route to a Gateway.
`hostnames` and `matches` choose which requests the rule handles; `backendRefs` says where they go.
For a Service backend, an implementation may target the Service IP or the Service's EndpointSlices.
Creating an HTTPRoute configures the underlying Gateway, e.g. extra routes in a cloud load balancer or proxy.
**GRPCRoute** works the same way for gRPC and can match on a gRPC `service` and `method`. Gateways that support it must support HTTP/2 without an initial upgrade from HTTP/1.

blocks.text: Exam check: a Route only takes effect once it points at the right Gateway via `parentRefs`, that Gateway names an existing class via `gatewayClassName`, and the listener's `allowedRoutes` admits the Route's namespace (same namespace by default).

sections.heading: Request flow and migrating from Ingress

blocks.text: A visitor looks up the host in the city directory and gets the gate's address. At the gate, the attendant (a reverse proxy) reads the visitor's Host header, finds the matching route card, optionally checks headers or path, optionally adjusts the visitor's paperwork (headers), then sends them to one or more destinations. Ports moving from the old main gate must convert their old rulebooks once; there is no old-gate form here.
For a Gateway implemented as a reverse proxy, an HTTP request goes like this:

items: 1. The client's DNS lookup for the host returns IP(s) belonging to the Gateway.
2. The client sends the request to that IP. The proxy uses the **Host header** to find config built from the Gateway and its attached HTTPRoute.
3. Optionally, the proxy matches on headers and/or path using the HTTPRoute's match rules.
4. Optionally, it modifies the request (e.g. adds or removes headers) using the HTTPRoute's filter rules.
5. It forwards the request to one or more backends.

blocks.text: Gateway API is the **successor to Ingress**, but it does not include an Ingress kind. Moving existing Ingress objects over needs a **one-time conversion** to Gateway API resources.
Because the API is broad and widely implemented, it has conformance definitions and tests (release channels, support levels) to keep behaviour consistent across implementations.

flashcards.front: Is Gateway API built into Kubernetes?
flashcards.back: No. It's an add-on defined as Custom Resources; install the CRDs or an implementation.

flashcards.front: The four stable Gateway API kinds?

flashcards.back: Infrastructure Provider, Cluster Operator, Application Developer.

flashcards.back: The implementation's controller assigns an address or hostname.

questions.stem: Which Gateway API kind represents an instance of traffic handling infrastructure, such as a cloud load balancer?

options.explanation: A Gateway defines an instance of traffic handling infrastructure.
GatewayClass defines a set of Gateways sharing config and a controller.
HTTPRoute holds HTTP routing rules from a listener to backends.
GRPCRoute holds gRPC routing rules.

questions.stem: Which are roles that Gateway API's role-oriented design is modelled on? Select 3.

options.explanation: Manages infrastructure serving multiple isolated clusters and tenants.
Manages clusters: policies, network access, app permissions.
Manages an application and its Service composition.
An ingress controller is software that fulfils Ingress objects, not one of the three Gateway API roles.

questions.stem: An HTTPRoute in namespace `team-a` references a Gateway in namespace `infra` whose listener has no allowedRoutes configured. What happens by default?

options.text: The Gateway does not accept the Route, because by default it only accepts Routes from its own namespace
options.explanation: Cross-namespace Routes require allowedRoutes on the listener.

options.text: The Route is accepted because parentRefs names the Gateway
options.explanation: Trust is bidirectional; the Gateway also filters which Routes may attach.

options.text: The Route is moved into the infra namespace automatically
options.explanation: Nothing moves objects between namespaces.
Route attachment is controlled on the Gateway listener via allowedRoutes.

questions.stem: Gateway API kinds are defined as Custom Resources, so you install the CRDs or an implementation before using them.

options.explanation: The page says the specs are Custom Resources, not natively implemented by Kubernetes.
Gateway API is an add-on; it is not built in.

questions.stem: Which field in an HTTPRoute links it to a Gateway?

options.explanation: parentRefs lists the Gateway(s) the Route attaches to.
backendRefs lists where matched traffic is sent, e.g. a Service.
That field is on a Gateway, pointing at its GatewayClass.
hostnames filters requests by host; it doesn't link to a Gateway.

questions.stem: Given an HTTPRoute with hostnames `www.example.com`, a PathPrefix match on `/login` and backendRef `example-svc` port 8080, which request reaches example-svc?

options.text: A request with Host www.example.com and path /login
options.explanation: Both the hostname and the path match, so it is routed to example-svc on 8080.
8080 is the backend port; matching uses host and path.

options.text: Any request for www.example.com, whatever the path
options.explanation: The rule also requires the /login path prefix.
HTTPRoute handles HTTP; GRPCRoute is for gRPC.

questions.stem: You're migrating to Gateway API. What happens to your existing Ingress objects?

options.text: You do a one-time conversion of them into Gateway API resources
options.explanation: Gateway API has no Ingress kind, so a one-time conversion is needed.

options.text: Gateway API serves them unchanged through its Ingress kind
options.explanation: Gateway API does not include the Ingress kind.
GatewayClass names a controller; it doesn't convert Ingress objects.

options.text: They must be deleted because Ingress is being removed
options.explanation: Gateway API is the successor, but the page only calls for converting them, not forced deletion.

questions.stem: In the documented request flow for a reverse-proxy Gateway, which steps are optional? Select 2.

options.text: Header and/or path matching based on HTTPRoute match rules
options.explanation: The flow lists matching as optional.

options.text: Modifying the request, e.g. adding or removing headers, using HTTPRoute filters
options.explanation: Request modification via filters is listed as optional.

options.text: Forwarding the request to one or more backends
options.explanation: Forwarding is the final step, not optional.

options.text: Using the Host header to find the matching configuration
options.explanation: The proxy always uses the Host header to pick config from the Gateway and HTTPRoute.

questions.stem: A single Gateway can be associated with several GatewayClasses at once.

options.explanation: A Gateway is associated with exactly one GatewayClass.
Correct: exactly one GatewayClass per Gateway.

questions.stem: Which design principle covers features like header-based matching and traffic weighting that Ingress only offered through custom annotations?

options.explanation: Expressive is about built-in support for common routing use cases.
Portable means the specs are custom resources supported by many implementations.
Extensible means custom resources can be linked at various API layers.
Role-oriented means the kinds mirror organisational roles.

questions.stem: A Gateway manifest has no `addresses` field. What happens?

options.text: The implementation's controller assigns an address or hostname
options.explanation: That's what the page describes for the example Gateway.

options.text: The Gateway is rejected as invalid
options.explanation: The documented example omits addresses and is valid.

options.text: It reuses the address of the cluster's Ingress controller
options.explanation: Gateway addresses come from the Gateway API implementation, not an Ingress controller.

options.text: The listener's hostname becomes the IP address
options.explanation: hostname filters traffic; the address is assigned by the controller.

questions.stem: What extra requirement applies to Gateways that support GRPCRoute?

options.text: They must support HTTP/2 without an initial upgrade from HTTP/1
options.explanation: This guarantees gRPC traffic flows properly.

options.text: They must be in the same namespace as every backend Service
options.explanation: The page sets no such namespace rule for GRPCRoute support.

options.text: They must not have any HTTPRoutes attached
options.explanation: Nothing on the page forbids mixing route kinds.
allowedRoutes controls which namespaces' Routes attach, not gRPC support.
